Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion Ghana’s electricity crisis: Falling fuel consumption is good news, but grid reliability remains a concern Source : Kojo Akoto Boateng 24 November 2026 7:07pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Over the past few weeks I have been a dashboard I built and call the National Electricity Intelligence Platform (NEiP). I built it to pull together everything electricity in Ghana. It’s a sub-dashboard within the bigger Ghana Energy Intelligence Platform.
Peak demand in 2025 hit 4,283 MW, an 8.4% jump on 2024. Total electricity consumption reached 27,015 GWh — above every Base Case projection.
But the cost was staggering. The 2025 plan budgeted for 344,387 barrels of Heavy Fuel Oil. The actual liquid fuel burned, according to the Energy Commission, reached 3,092,066 barrels — nearly 9 times what was planned.
AKSA alone burned 1,040,335 barrels of HFO. SAPP and Cenpower between them burned nearly 2.3 million barrels of LCO and DFO combined.
Natural gas supply fell 5.3% short. To keep the lights on, the grid turned to the most expensive fuels on the planet. We paid for the liquid fuels in scarce foreign exchange and that new levy that was imposed on us.
Last night, when I was going through the National Petroleum Authority's January–September 2026 supply data, I saw some good news. The data showed power plants consumed only 14,269 metric tonnes of Fuel Oil and just 1,441 metric tonnes of Diesel across nine months. This means that the fuel levy is not needed again because we have reduced our dependence on liquid fuel.
AKSA alone burned the equivalent of roughly 142,000 MT of HFO in 2025. If the Jan–Sep 2026 pace holds through Q4, power-sector liquid fuel consumption this year will land at around 10% of 2025 levels. Costs will reduce and the levy must go.
NPA's Q2 2026 bulletin confirms the same direction of travel for fuel imports. Fuel Oil imports fell 76.22% year-on-year against Q2 2025.
Natural gas supply has materially improved in 2026. Whether through better WAGP flows, higher N-Gas imports, or firmer Jubilee/TEN/Sankofa production, I don’t know. The 2027 Energy and Electricity Supply plans will tell us. What makes me happy is that the single biggest driver of our 2025 fuel bill pain appears to have eased. If this holds, Ghana will spend substantially less on thermal fuel in 2026 than the Energy Commission's worst-case US$1.68 billion projection. So the levy must go!
Easing gas supply does not mean the grid is fixed. The Energy Commission's 2026 Outlook (published this February) warned that dependable capacity (5,455 MW) would fall below the 18% Grid Code reserve margin in 11 of 12 months this year.
Only August cleared the bar in the commission’s projections.
Under the High Case, the margin turned negative in February, March, April, May and June.
Then 23 April 2026 arrived. A fire at the Akosombo switchyard removed 1,020 MW of hydro plus 101 MW at Kpong in a single afternoon. About 23% of national peak demand was erased in one incident. The whole grid shutdown. Recovery took 11 days through novel external switchyard injection. All six units are now fully restored.
That fire laid bare a single-point-of-failure risk we have no redundancy for.
GRIDCo's 2025 ESP finally quantified what engineers in the field have long known. At Kadjebi substation, voltage drops to 38.5 kV on a 69 kV nominal network — just 56% of what consumers should receive.
Towns like Bimbila, Kpandai, Salaga and Kete Krachi are served by 34.5 kV feeders running more than 200 km from Yendi. Motors cannot start, fridges cannot cool and industrial equipment trip.
GRIDCo quantified the suppressed demand on NEDCo feeders alone to be 25.78 MW / 151.3 GWh of electricity Ghanaians would consume if the grid could deliver it reliably. Historical NEDCo data shows that when voltages on affected feeders are improved, consumption rises 24%. That is demand nobody is counting.
NEDCo’s operational area demand is small compared to ECG’s so if voltage improvement increases consumption by 24%, just imagine what that would do in the ECG operational areas.
GRIDCo projects peak demand to rise from 4,283 MW (2025) to 6,198 MW by 2030. That is a 1,915 MW jump in five years. To hold reliability at the Grid Code's 18% reserve margin, Ghana must commission an average of 374 MW of new dependable generation every single year.
AKSA Anwomaso began operating in December 2025. CENIT Anwomaso came online in April 2026. The Yendi 50 MW solar came in July.
This is all good but nowhere near enough. If the proposed New Economy can take off, the current need must be met with enough produced to power the New Economy.
The Bridge Power Phase II, Rotan 600 MW, SAAP Solar 200 MW, KTPP combined-cycle — every one of these has to deliver on time, or we enter 2030 already short.
When are we commissioning the 400 mmscfd regasification Tema LNG facility? Or its been done and we didn’t notice?.
Suppressed demand is real. The adundum adundum is happening. The low voltage is widespread.
It would be great to hear from the government the compressing electricity RESET programme and how that would solve our problems.
What we measure, we can manage. What we cannot see, we cannot fix.
Sources: National Petroleum Authority Jan–Sep 2026 National Supply · NPA Q2 2026 Downstream Petroleum Statistical Bulletin · Energy Commission 2026 Energy Outlook for Ghana (February 2026) · GRIDCo 2025 Electricity Supply Plan · GRIDCo Daily System Load Reports.
